title: Occlumency
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
My first lesson in Occlumency began with Snape telling me not to trust him.

“Comforting,” I said.

“Necessary.”

We were in the research laboratory after hours. The doors were locked. The fireplace was out. No potion simmered between us to provide an excuse for attention.

Snape stood across the room with his wand lowered.

“If I enter your mind, your instinct will be to follow whatever image rises,” he said. “Do not. Observe the intrusion. Do not assist it.”

“You make thoughts sound like unhelpful houseguests.”

“Yours are.”

I ignored that.

“Can you see everything?”

“No.”

“Can you choose what you see?”

“To a degree.”

“Can I stop you?”

“That is the point.”

“Can you stop if I tell you to?”

His expression changed.

“Yes.”

“Immediately?”

“Yes.”

“Then that's the rule.”

“It was already the rule.”

“I need to hear you say it.”

A pause.

Snape nodded.

“If you tell me to stop, I stop.”

Only then did I raise my wand.

He noticed the sequence.

Of course he did.

“You do not trust me,” he said.

“I trust you enough to try.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

Something like approval crossed his face.

“Good.”

The first attempt lasted less than a second.

“Legilimens.”

The room vanished.

A flash of light.

A door.

My own laughter.

A fear I had not invited.

I shoved mentally at everything at once.

Snape was gone immediately.

I staggered.

He did not catch me.

Rule.

I steadied myself on the table.

“Terrible,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“You attempted to suppress the memories.”

“What else was I supposed to do?”

“Detach.”

“That is not an instruction.”

“It is the only instruction that matters.”

I glared.

His mouth twitched.

“Again.”

The second attempt lasted two seconds.

The third, four.

By the fifth, I learned the difference between hiding a thought and refusing to chase it.

Snape entered.

An image rose.

I let it pass.

Another.

I let it pass.

Then his own face appeared in my mind.

Not from the present.

Hogsmeade rain.

His little finger hooking around mine beneath the umbrella.

My concentration shattered.

Snape broke the spell instantly.

We stared at each other.

He had seen it.

I knew he had.

Color rose beneath his sallow skin.

“Well,” I said.

His voice was extremely controlled. “Your defenses remain inadequate.”

“That's what you took from that?”

“You followed the memory.”

“You were in it.”

“Which is irrelevant.”

“It was relevant to me.”

His eyes flashed.

The tension shifted.

Not embarrassment now.

Awareness.

“Again,” he said.

I lifted my wand.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“You may see worse.”

“I am aware.”

“You may see better.”

His jaw tightened.

“I am aware.”

I smiled faintly.

“Stop enjoying this.”

“I am not.”

“Liar.”

“Close your mind.”

He cast.

This time I was ready for him.

Memories rose.

I did not chase them.

A room.

A voice.

A hand in mine.

The first time I saw Snape smile.

The thought tried to pull me toward it.

I let it float past.

Then something darker rose.

A private grief.

I felt Snape retreat before I asked.

The spell ended.

I opened my eyes.

He had moved half a step backward.

“Why did you stop?”

“Your concentration broke.”

“No. It didn't.”

His face hardened.

“You saw something you decided not to enter.”

“I told you I can choose to a degree.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

He looked away.

I understood.

He had found a boundary I had not named and treated it as real anyway.

Trust shifted again.

Small.

Precise.

Like an ingredient added at the correct second.

“Thank you,” I said.

His mouth tightened.

“Do not thank me for basic ethics.”

“Plenty of people fail them.”

“That does not make success exceptional.”

“Fine. I won't praise you.”

“Good.”

“You were decent.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Worse.”

I laughed.

We took a break.

Snape brewed tea while I sat on the edge of a table and tried to settle my thoughts.

“Is this how you hid from Voldemort?” I asked.

He paused.

“In part.”

“What did you do with the memories you couldn't afford him seeing?”

“Contained them.”

“How?”

“Practice.”

“That is annoyingly vague.”

“It is also true.”

He handed me tea.

I took it.

“Were you afraid every time he looked at you?”

Snape's eyes went still.

I almost withdrew the question.

Then he said, “Yes.”

The honesty landed hard.

“He was better at Legilimency than I was.”

“Better?”

“More powerful. Less restrained.”

“How did you keep him out?”

“I did not keep him out.”

I stared.

Snape sat opposite me.

“That is the mistake most people make when imagining Occlumency. A perfect wall is suspicious. I allowed him access to what I wanted him to find.”

The implication made my skin cold.

“You built lies out of real memories.”

“Yes.”

“You let him see enough truth to believe the rest.”

“Yes.”

“For years.”

“Yes.”

I looked at him differently then.

Not admiringly.

With horror at the endurance it required.

“Did you know who you were after a while?”

His eyes snapped to mine.

The question had escaped unplanned.

I expected anger.

Instead he looked tired.

“Sometimes,” he said.

The word sat between us.

I set down the cup.

“Can I touch you?”

His gaze sharpened, then softened by a fraction.

“Yes.”

I held out my hand.

He took it.

No drama.

No mark exposed.

Just fingers closing around mine.

“I know who you are now,” I said.

His face changed.

“That is an extraordinary claim.”

“I didn't say I know everything.”

“Then clarify.”

“I know who you are when you're with me.”

His thumb moved over my knuckle.

“And who is that?”

“A man who drinks terrible tea, weaponizes vocabulary, cheats at emotional conversations, and bought me very good gloves.”

His mouth curved.

“Trivial.”

“Exactly.”

The smile faded into something softer.

I squeezed his hand.

“Not a spy. Not a Death Eater. Not a martyr. Not Lily's tragedy. Just you, for an hour.”

Snape looked at our hands.

“That sounds dangerous.”

“Probably.”

He did not let go.

When we resumed Occlumency, I lasted almost ten seconds.

The final memory that rose was Snape's hand in mine.

This time I let it pass without following.

When the spell ended, he looked almost proud.

“Better,” he said.

I smiled.

The next lesson, Severus put a bowl of water on the desk between us.

I looked at it. “Are we hydrating?”

“We are establishing a recovery cue.”

That sounded suspiciously healthy.

He ignored my expression.

“If you become disoriented after contact, you will place both hands around the bowl and name five observable properties.”

“Cold, wet, round—”

“During the exercise.”

“You're no fun.”

“I am teaching you to prevent magical intrusion from becoming panic.”

“Yes, Professor.”

His eyes narrowed.

The exercise went badly twice and well once. On the fourth attempt, I lost track of the room entirely and came out gasping.

Severus did not reach for me.

“Bowl,” he said.

I found it.

“Five things.”

“Cold. Ceramic. Blue. Chipped at the rim. Heavier than it looks.”

“Four.”

“That's five.”

“Heavier is an inference.”

I glared at him.

The room snapped fully back into focus.

His mouth twitched.

“You did that on purpose.”

“Anger is grounding.”

“That is the most Severus Snape therapeutic technique imaginable.”

“I am not your therapist.”

“Thank Merlin.”

He almost smiled.

More importantly, he had brought me back without taking control away from me.

This time he allowed it.
